extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and practitioners of scientific method, philosophy of science, and experimental research
extracted.subtask_description: Statements and canons describing five principal experimental methods (Difference, Agreement, Joint/Indirect Difference, Residues, Concomitant Variations) and the conditions, precautions, and limitations that justify causal inferences from observation and experiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Difference
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare a pre-existing state of circumstances with a state produced by introducing the phenomenon (A) so that the two states differ in nothing except the presence or absence of that phenomenon; repetition gives assurance that no other circumstance has supervened.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best applied when we can modify or control phenomena by voluntary agency (artificial experiment). Beware the possibility that the effect was produced not by the change itself but by the means used to produce the change; test this by other experiments. The requisitions of this method (instances agreeing in every antecedent except A or every consequent except a) are seldom fulfilled in purely spontaneous observations but are generally satisfiable in controlled experiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Agreement
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine any instances in which a phenomenon occurs; if all such instances agree in some circumstance (A), then that circumstance is connected with the phenomenon (an invariable antecedent or consequent), yielding a law of phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This method often yields uniformities but does not by itself establish causation or direction (whether A is cause or a is effect). It is chiefly useful where artificial experiment is impossible and as a means to suggest applications of the Method of Difference. To determine causation direction one must be able to produce the effect by means of the antecedent or obtain an instance with the effect where no other antecedent changed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint Method of Agreement and Difference (Indirect Method of Difference)
rubrics_metrics.description: A double employment of the Method of Agreement: if instances where the phenomenon occurs have only one circumstance in common, and instances where it does not occur agree only in the absence of that circumstance, the differing circumstance is the cause, effect, or necessary part of the cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expressed as the THIRD CANON in the text: 'If two or more instances in which the phenomenon occurs have only one circumstance in common, while two or more instances in which it does not occur have nothing in common save the absence of that circumstance; the circumstance in which alone the two sets of instances differ, is the effect, or cause, or a necessary part of the cause, of the phenomenon.' This method extends and improves the Method of Agreement but is not equivalent to the direct Method of Difference and does not satisfy its stricter requisitions unless exclusivity of antecedents/consequents can be assured.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Residues
rubrics_metrics.description: Subtract from a given phenomenon the parts which, by previous inductions, can be assigned to known causes; the remainder (residue) is the effect of the remaining antecedents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stated as the FOURTH CANON: 'Subduct from any phenomenon such part as is known by previous inductions to be the effect of certain antecedents, and the residue of the phenomenon is the effect of the remaining antecedents.' This is a form of the Method of Difference and partakes of its certainty only if the previous inductions were obtained by an infallible method and if one can be sure the residual antecedent is the only remaining cause. Otherwise the residue must be tested by obtaining the antecedent artificially or by deductive account from known laws. Despite limits, the method is highly fertile for discovering obscure causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Concomitant Variations
rubrics_metrics.description: When one phenomenon varies in any manner whenever another varies in some particular manner, the two are either cause and effect or connected through causation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expressed as the FIFTH CANON: 'Whatever phenomenon varies in any manner whenever another phenomenon varies in some particular manner, is either a cause or an effect of that phenomenon, or is connected with it through some fact of causation.' Must beware that concomitance does not by itself determine direction (they may be distinct effects of a common cause); attempt to produce one set of variations by means of the other to resolve direction. Concomitance itself should, where possible, be corroborated by the Method of Difference. Particularly useful for quantitative laws (numerical relations between cause and effect) but requires knowledge of absolute quantities and other precautions when extrapolating (e.g., not to infer unjustified limits like contraction to zero).

rubrics_metrics.name: Control of other antecedents (experimental control)
rubrics_metrics.description: To warrant inferring causation from variation in one antecedent, endeavour to retain all other antecedents unchanged while subjecting that particular antecedent to the requisite series of variations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This precaution is repeatedly emphasized as necessary across the methods (Difference, Concomitant Variations, etc.). Without holding other antecedents fixed, observed correlations may be confounded and inferences invalid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Produce antecedent (or obtain 'negative' instance) to determine direction
rubrics_metrics.description: To decide whether an invariable antecedent is a cause (or an invariable consequent an effect), one must be able to produce the one by means of the other, or obtain an instance in which the effect appears with no other change but the presence of the alleged antecedent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If direct experimentation is impossible, the joint method (agreement + agreement on absence) or other indirect proofs may approximate the requisite evidence; but without some means of showing that addition or removal of A produces or removes a, the question of causation/direction remains undecided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variation/modification method for Permanent Causes
rubrics_metrics.description: When a permanent cause cannot be excluded or isolated (it is always present), determine its effects by producing or observing modifications in it (in quantity or spatial relations) and assessing corresponding changes in the phenomenon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used when exclusion is impossible (e.g., heat, the earth's influence, the moon). By observing how variations (quantity, position) of the permanent cause correlate with variations of the effect, one may infer causal influence. This approach underlies the Method of Concomitant Variations and requires attention to whether variations are in quantity or relations (position) and to the possibility of common causes.
